beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Here is a division that looks big. Ninety-six divided by four.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Ninety-six? That is not in my four times table!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: True. But you do not need ninety-six in your table. You only need facts you already know, used one chunk at a time.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Picture a rectangle, four squares tall. All of these squares have to fill it. How long must it be?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: So four times something has to make ninety-six.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Yes! That missing side is the answer to the division. Let us build the rectangle one easy chunk at a time.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: First, a chunk ten long. Four times ten is forty. Watch forty squares leave the pile and line up.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Forty used. Ninety-six take away forty leaves fifty-six.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Another chunk of ten, another forty. Sixteen left.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Four times what makes sixteen?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Four times four! That one is in my table!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Yes. A chunk four long uses every square.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Empty! Now read the missing side along the top: ten, ten, and four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Ten plus ten plus four is twenty-four. So ninety-six divided by four equals twenty-four.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: And I only used my table! Four times ten, and four times four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now build the very same rectangle with different chunks. Who wants a bigger bite?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Twenty! Four times twenty is eighty. That is in my table too.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Sixteen left. Sixteen is four times four. One more chunk, four long.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Twenty plus four. Twenty-four, again!

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Different chunks, but the same length!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Always. Pick chunks that feel easy, but never one that goes over. Thirty fours is one hundred twenty, which is too many.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Here is a quick way to see it, too. Twenty-five fours make one hundred.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Ninety-six is one four less than one hundred. So it takes one four fewer: twenty-four of them.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now a much bigger one. Eight hundred fifty-two divided by six.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Same idea: a rectangle six tall. We squeeze the picture to fit, but the numbers stay true. Start with the biggest chunk that does not go over.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Six times one hundred is six hundred. Two hundreds would be twelve hundred, too many. So, one hundred.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A chunk one hundred long. Six hundred squares line up, and two hundred fifty-two are left.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Tens now. Six times fifty is three hundred, too many. Six times forty is two hundred forty, so forty fits.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A chunk forty long. Two hundred forty squares line up. Twelve are left.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Twelve is two sixes! Six times two.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Yes. One last chunk, two long, and the pile is gone.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One hundred plus forty plus two is one hundred forty-two. So eight hundred fifty-two divided by six is one hundred forty-two.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Sometimes the pile does not empty exactly. Try fifty-nine divided by four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Same rectangle, four tall. A chunk ten long: forty squares line up. Nineteen are left.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Four times four is sixteen, so a chunk four long. Three are left.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Can three squares make one more column? A column here is four tall.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Three is not enough. One square short!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Right. Those three are the remainder, what is left over when no full column fits. Fifty-nine divided by four is fourteen, remainder three.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Could the remainder be four? No! With four squares, the column is whole, and we take one more.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: So the remainder is always smaller than the number you divide by. Here, smaller than four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Check it by multiplying back. Four times fourteen is fifty-six. Add the three left over: fifty-nine.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Or start from a friendly number. Fifteen fours make sixty, just one more than fifty-nine.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Sixty is too many, so take one four away. Fourteen fours make fifty-six, and three are left over.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Here is where many of us slip. Eight hundred twenty-four divided by four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Two hundred first. Four times two hundred is eight hundred. Twenty-four are left.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Tens? Four times ten is forty, but only twenty-four are left. Too many!

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: So there is no tens chunk at all!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Right. Zero tens. The ghost goes away, and the tens place holds a zero.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Ones: four times six is twenty-four. A chunk six long uses every square.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Two hundred plus zero plus six makes two hundred six in all.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: I almost wrote twenty-six!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: That is the trap. The zero holds the tens place. Two hundred six, not twenty-six.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One more, with four digits. Three thousand six hundred twelve divided by three.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A thousand first. Three times a thousand is three thousand. Six hundred twelve are left.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Two hundred next. Three times two hundred is six hundred. Twelve are left.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Tens? Three times ten is thirty, more than twelve. So zero tens again. Then four: three fours make twelve.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One thousand plus two hundred plus zero plus four is one thousand two hundred four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: So here is the whole idea in one picture. A rectangle four tall, with ninety-six squares inside.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Three chunks from facts you know: forty, forty, and sixteen. Their lengths are ten, ten, and four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Add the lengths, and you have the missing side: twenty-four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Build the rectangle in chunks you know. Add up the lengths. And whatever is left over, too small to make one more column, is the remainder.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Chunks, lengths, remainder. Now I can divide anything!
